statement: Ben has lots of 5-cent coins and 2-cent coins. How many different mixes of these coins make exactly 20 cents? A mix can use just one kind of coin.

choices.misconception: I found four 5-cent coins and ten 2-cent coins, but missed the way that uses both kinds.
I also counted one 5-cent coin, without checking that the 15 cents left cannot be made from 2-cent coins.
I counted 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 five-cent coins without checking whether the rest could be made from 2-cent coins.
I gave the number of 2-cent coins in the mix that uses only 2-cent coins.

hints: Try each number of 5-cent coins in turn.
List the mixes by how many 5-cent coins they use: 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4. For each one, check whether the cents left over can be made exactly from 2-cent coins.
2-cent coins can only make even amounts. With 1 or 3 five-cent coins the amount left over is odd.

solutions.reliable: Go through the 5-cent coins. 0 fives: 20 cents left, ten 2-cent coins. 1 five: 15 left, odd, impossible. 2 fives: 10 left, five 2-cent coins. 3 fives: 5 left, odd, impossible. 4 fives: 0 left. So there are 3 mixes. The idea to keep: list the cases in order and check each one, because some cases are impossible.
solutions.elegant: 2-cent coins always make an even amount, so the 5-cent coins must also make an even amount: 0, 10 or 20 cents. That is 3 mixes.

whyOnTest: Making an amount with two coin types rewards a careful list, and the odd leftover is the hidden check that rules cases out.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
